summary:
External research digest (8 sourced claims; no project evidence used)

1. Claim: “Enough testing” should be defined by residual product risk, not by a universal test count or blanket coverage percentage. Risk level combines likelihood and impact; the analysis should determine scope, test levels, test types, techniques, coverage targets, effort, and priority. Microsoft likewise says to scale coverage by risk and value and not overinvest in one flow past diminishing returns. Direct source URLs: https://istqb.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/ISTQB_CTFL_Syllabus_v4.0.1.pdf (sections 5.2.1–5.2.4); https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/testing (“Scale coverage strategically”). Publishers: International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB); Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework. Publication/update dates: ISTQB v4.0.1 formally released 2024-09-15; Microsoft page dated 2026-07-30, metadata updated 2026-08-04. Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High. Claim class: recognized testing reference + current vendor engineering guidance.

2. Claim: Layer tests by the smallest scope that can prove the behavior. Unit tests prove individual rules/components in isolation; integration/API/contract tests prove component, service, database, API, and consumer-contract interactions; browser E2E proves a full user workflow across the system. A complete vertical journey is warranted when a feature creates or changes a critical user goal/core business path, because isolated feature tests do not prove that the tasks compose into a working workflow. Google explicitly calls these Critical User Journeys and recommends E2E for them; Microsoft describes E2E as correctness from user action through backend services and says to use it selectively for business-critical flows. Direct source URLs: https://testing.googleblog.com/2021/06/how-much-testing-is-enough.html; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/testing. Publishers: Google Testing Blog (Google); Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework. Publication/update dates: 2021-06-15; 2026-07-30 (metadata updated 2026-08-04). Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High. Claim class: primary industry engineering guidance.

3. Claim: The pyramid is a portfolio-shape heuristic, not a quota. Google’s older 70/20/10 split is explicitly only a “good first guess” whose exact mix varies by team. Google’s newer SMURF guidance says a growing suite must go beyond the pyramid and balance Speed, Maintainability, Utilization, Reliability, and Fidelity: smaller tests usually win on the first four, while integration/E2E gain fidelity. Therefore, a mature gate should justify expensive tests by unique risk coverage rather than enforce a fixed numerical ratio. Direct source URLs: https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html; https://testing.googleblog.com/2024/10/smurf-beyond-test-pyramid.html. Publisher: Google Testing Blog (Google). Publication/update dates: 2015-04-22; 2024-10-15. Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High for the guidance; Medium for any attempt to generalize the illustrative ratio. Claim class: engineering heuristic and later refinement.

4. Claim: Behavior partitioning is the first defense against Cartesian explosion. ISTQB defines equivalence partitions as values expected to be processed alike, for which one representative per partition is sufficient; boundaries deserve separate coverage because faults cluster there. For interacting business conditions, decision tables identify feasible outcome rules, but when rules grow exponentially ISTQB explicitly permits a minimized table or risk-based selection. Direct source URL: https://istqb.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/ISTQB_CTFL_Syllabus_v4.0.1.pdf (sections 4.1–4.2.3). Publisher: ISTQB. Publication/update date: 2024-09-15. Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High. Claim class: recognized testing technique/reference.

5. Claim: Stateful features need transition-oriented coverage, not merely one example per visible state. ISTQB distinguishes all-states coverage, valid-transition coverage, and all-transitions coverage (including attempted invalid transitions); valid-transition coverage is stronger than all-states coverage, and all-transitions is identified as a minimum for mission- and safety-critical software. A single sequence can economically cover several transitions. Direct source URL: https://istqb.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/ISTQB_CTFL_Syllabus_v4.0.1.pdf (section 4.2.4). Publisher: ISTQB. Publication/update date: 2024-09-15. Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High. Claim class: model-based behavioral coverage reference.

6. Claim: Roles and identities are separate behavioral dimensions when authorization or ownership changes the outcome. OWASP requires testing unauthenticated and post-logout access, cross-role/privilege access (vertical authorization), and cross-identity access between two users with the same privilege (horizontal authorization). Consequently, “ordinary user” is not one sufficient class for resource-owning features: owner and non-owner identities can be distinct equivalence classes even under the same role. Direct source URL: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/v42/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization_Testing/02-Testing_for_Bypassing_Authorization_Schema.html. Publisher: OWASP Foundation, Web Security Testing Guide v4.2. Publication/update date: v4.2 released 2020-12-03 (release record: https://owasp.org/2020/12/03/wstg-v42-released; the individual stable page does not state a per-page date). Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High. Claim class: security testing reference.

7. Claim: Pairwise/t-way covering arrays are an economical alternative to exhaustive combinations, but pairwise is not a universal sufficiency claim. NIST found that faults often involve few factors; in one NASA subject, 2-way combinations triggered 93% of observed failures and 3-way 98%, with the studied systems reaching 100% at strengths 4–6. The same guide warns pairwise may miss 10–40% or more of system bugs and is insufficient for mission-critical software. It also notes that continuous inputs must first be discretized and that generated inputs are useless without a trustworthy expected-result oracle. Direct source URL: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/142/final (publication PDF linked there). Publisher: U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, SP 800-142. Publication date: 2010-10-07 (October 2010). Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High for the reported subjects and method limits; Medium for extrapolation to a new product. Claim class: empirical research + government technical guidance.

8. Claim: More E2E tests—or more tests generally—can reduce gate quality when they add latency, flakiness, duplicate coverage, or poor diagnosability. Google’s experience-based account reports E2E-dominant suites hiding small bugs behind large failures, producing flaky results, and delaying feedback; it recommends a small E2E layer above focused integration tests. Microsoft calls E2E high-cost and fragile, says larger suites do not always yield meaningful ROI, recommends critical flows only, and states that a smaller reliable suite is more valuable than a large flaky one. This is the requested contrary evidence against “test every path in the browser” and against equating volume with assurance. Direct source URLs: https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/testing. Publishers: Google Testing Blog (Google); Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework. Publication/update dates: 2015-04-22; 2026-07-30 (metadata updated 2026-08-04). Access date: 2026-09-10. Confidence: High that the trade-off is recognized by both organizations; Medium for Google’s operational evidence because it is a composite of practitioner experiences rather than a controlled study. Claim class: contrary operational evidence + current engineering guidance.

files.description: Google guidance on unit/integration/E2E allocation, Critical User Journeys, behavior coverage, and risk.
Google’s E2E-heavy-suite failure pattern, pyramid heuristic, and 70/20/10-as-first-guess caveat.
Google’s newer multidimensional suite-balancing heuristic: speed, maintainability, utilization, reliability, fidelity.
Current Microsoft guidance on layer responsibilities, risk/value scaling, critical workflows, test ROI, and pipeline use.
Recognized testing reference for equivalence partitions, decision tables, state transitions, pyramid, risk analysis, and prioritization.
NIST SP 800-142 on pairwise/t-way combinatorial testing, empirical interaction strengths, costs, and limitations.
OWASP stable authorization testing guidance for unauthenticated, cross-role, and cross-identity cases.
Official publication record dating OWASP WSTG v4.2 to 2020-12-03.

architecture:
Recommended generalized sufficiency model [INFERENCE synthesized from the cited guidance]

Use a feature-risk manifest rather than an unconditional scenario matrix. For each changed observable behavior, record: critical user goal; likelihood × impact; partitions/boundaries; starting and ending states plus valid/invalid transitions; role, authentication, ownership/tenant identities; external/component boundaries; configuration factors; and required evidence layer.

Layer allocation:
- Unit/component: exhaustively cover cheap deterministic rules—calculations, validation partitions and boundaries, decision outcomes, pure state-machine transitions, permission-policy functions, and error mapping.
- Integration/API/contract: prove behavior whose risk lives at boundaries—API contracts, service/database persistence, authorization enforcement, ownership/tenant separation, state-transition side effects, dependency failures, serialization, and transaction semantics. Put most role × state × data variants here rather than in the browser.
- Browser E2E: require at least one complete user-action-to-system-result journey when the change affects a critical user goal/core business workflow or when the principal risk is that UI, routing, backend, persistence, and displayed result fail to compose. Add browser variants only for materially different user-visible outcomes or high-risk browser-specific behavior; do not repeat every lower-layer value combination.

Economic variant selection:
1. Remove infeasible combinations and explicitly encode constraints.
2. Cover every behavior equivalence class and risk-relevant boundary at the cheapest trustworthy layer.
3. Cover distinct decision outcomes and required transitions, not every raw input tuple.
4. For remaining nominal independent factors, use pairwise as a sampling baseline.
5. Escalate selected high-risk interactions to 3-way or higher, or targeted exhaustive coverage, when domain knowledge, incident history, security boundaries, mission criticality, or coupled implementation makes pairwise’s assumptions unsafe.
6. Always preserve explicit must-test cases (critical journey, privileged denial, cross-tenant/owner denial, destructive transition, recovery path); do not let a covering-array generator sample them away.

Fail-closed pre-merge gate:
- The gate should fail if any risk-declared required evidence is missing, skipped without an accepted rationale, flaky/unreliable, or failing. It should not accept a pass-rate threshold that tolerates arbitrary failed required tests.
- Base and middle layers run on changes for fast isolation; the small, selected vertical journeys run when applicable. “Not applicable” must be traceable to the risk manifest, not inferred from test absence.
- Sufficiency is achieved when every identified material risk maps to a passing proof at an appropriate layer and the residual risk is explicitly accepted—not when all Cartesian combinations or a fixed test-count/code-coverage target are reached.

Contradictions/tensions:
- Google 2015 offers 70/20/10 as an initial shape, while Google 2024 says the pyramid alone is insufficient at scale. Reconciliation: keep the pyramid bias, but tune the mix through SMURF and feature risk rather than enforce the ratio.
- Microsoft says E2E provides the highest overall-confidence/fidelity view, while Google and Microsoft both warn it is slow, costly, fragile, and hard to diagnose. Reconciliation: retain a small complete-journey set for risks no lower layer can prove.
- Pairwise is a common economical approach, but NIST directly warns that it can miss 10–40% or more and is inadequate for mission-critical systems. Reconciliation: use pairwise as a baseline, not a release guarantee; raise interaction strength selectively by risk.

Leads:
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4, referenced by ISTQB, for the formal specification of test-design techniques.
- NIST ACTS, linked by SP 800-142, for constraint-aware t-way covering-array generation.
- OWASP ASVS authorization requirements, referenced by WSTG, for a normative actor/resource/action coverage inventory.

Gaps:
- No authoritative source supplies a universal numeric threshold for “sufficient”; the cited guidance deliberately leaves thresholds to product risk and organizational risk appetite.
- NIST’s interaction percentages are empirical results from specific systems, not a guarantee for future features; factor independence, discretization, constraints, and oracle quality remain design work.
- The sources do not prescribe a universal PR runtime budget, exact flake policy, or risk-tier-to-layer table. Those must be locally defined, but the fail-closed rule can still require all evidence selected by that policy to be present and green.
